articles.headline: Moralizing.
articles.text:
Born of the active, rustling life of the west, is an unreasoning impatience at delay, the effect of which is almost wholly evil. Some town, for instance, is boomed in the nervous, energetic way peculiar to the west. No account is taken of the resources a town must have to be successful. A set of men make up their minds that there is to be a good town in a certain place and, seeing the prospect they proceed to make one in advance of the order. Buildings out of all reason are hurried up, stores established and soon a town blossoms out, fair to the eye but consisting only of an outer shell,—an appearance. Like the bodies of some microscopic beings, consisting only of a stomach, they are non-producers; only useful to themselves. As soon as the supply of food or suckers ceases they fairly turn themselves inside out in their search for food or complain bitterly that some good Samaritan does not rescue them from the fire which they have kindled about themselves.

There is no use denying or rather attempting to deny the open secret that the above is the history of a large number of Dakota towns. They are years and years ahead of their surrounding country. We can point to fifty towns which must depend entirely on agriculture for existence and have from ten to fifty per cent more invested in the townsite than in tributary farming improvements. This is getting the cart before the horse with a vengeance. It stands to reason that these towns cannot be immediately prosperous. It is as impossible for them to remain stationary and they will surely retrograde until the surrounding country catches up with them.

Then the silly fool who in search of the almighty dollar, have been decoyed into the embrace of the boomer, sits supinely down and curses the country for not growing faster. The time will surely come when all these towns will be prosperous, but it may be "after many years," at least not until the surrounding country is thickly settled. You must first find your goose before you can get one to lay golden eggs. The boomer's plan of finding a counterfeit goose and selling it to the tenderfoot to kill in search of golden eggs is peach and honey to the boomer but yields only withered leaves for the pilgrims share.

The moral of this whole thing is that there are more consumers than producers in these towns and as long as this state of affairs exists, so long will they be worse than dead.

It might seem invidious in this connection to speak of Medora, but as she is emphatically not an agricultural town, it will be proper to mention her by way of contrast. She depends in no way on the uncertainties of a harvest,—the calf crop is as certain as the everlasting hills. Our growth so far has not been equal to the demand and this is the reason why every business interest here is flourishing. Merely as a cattle town our future is assured. The freight line is now doing much and in the future will do more for our advancement. The stage line, which is hanging fire only because the proper man has not been found to place in charge, will be an entering wedge for the railroad, which will make Medora the distributing point for the whole Black Hills and intermediate country. Without railroad, freight or stage lines, Medora can look forward to a constant, steady and successful growth. With them, she will be the best town in Dakota, west of the Missouri.

But even here the voice of the complainer is heard and there is a constant desire to start a boom. What, we would like to know, would be the permanent advantage derived thereby? There is an abundance of capital ready for investment here and our voice always has been and always will be raised against its use in advance of the needs of the place. We are certain of having enough invested to keep pace with the times. Any invested beyond this will be followed by a corresponding reaction. "Rome was not made in a day," nor will the impression go abroad that Medora's future prosperity can be accomplished in any such short time if we can help it.

We never have and never will claim anything for Medora that we do not believe is absolutely and unqualifiedly true. We don't want a boomed town and won't have it as long as "the voice of the Cow Boy reverberates from butte to butte," as a sap-headed contemporary puts it. "Legitimate growth" is our path to prosperity.
articles.summary: Packard's editorial against town 'booming' in Dakota, contrasting over-built agricultural towns with Medora as a cattle town whose growth rests on the calf crop, the freight line and a hoped-for stage line to the Black Hills.

articles.text: Johnny Goodall and J. L. Truscott came in from Beaver creek yesterday morning, at the close of the round-up. It lasted just a month and was a great success, especially considering the fact that it was the first round-up for this district. No dispute or dissatisfaction of any kind arose and everything moved like clockwork. The district rounded up averages one hundred by fifty miles and contains between 30,000 and 40,000 cattle. The cattle are in excellent condition, most of them being ready for slaughter. The calf crop is lighter than was expected, the highest estimate for the district being 75 per cent. and the lowest 55. This is doubtless owing to the fact that bulls have been allowed to range with the herd the year round. Under an association, this evil will be remedied, as it is a prime necessity in this climate to keep the bulls up from November till July at least, longer would be better.
articles.summary: Goodall and Truscott return from Beaver creek at the close of the district's first round-up, which lasted a month and covered 30,000 to 40,000 cattle.

articles.text: A number of the outfits represented on our round-up will send cowboys to search Cabin, Glendive and Cedar creeks for stray cattle.
articles.summary: Round-up outfits will send cowboys to hunt strays on Cabin, Glendive and Cedar creeks.

articles.text: At a fair calculation the stock growers of Colorado have invested in bulls nearly, if not quite, two million dollars. Nine-tenths of all these animals are grades.—[Denver L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping: Colorado stockmen's investment in bulls.

articles.text: Clark & Plum, of the E6 ranch, will sell several thousand head of fat cattle this year. About 10,000 head of Texas cattle are on the drive for them from their Texas ranches. From conversations with Mr. Clark, we judge that a number of steers will be sent into the Bad Lands near here, for fattening.
articles.summary: Clark & Plum of the E6 ranch will sell fat cattle and have about 10,000 Texas cattle on the drive; some steers may come to the Bad Lands.

articles.text: A hundred thousand fat steers, four years old and upward will be the beef crop of Colorado the coming fall. Five thousand cars will be required to carry them to market. If the railroads will but give the flock owners double decks and a liberal rate a thousand cars of fat muttons will also go forward.—[Denver L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping: Colorado's expected fall beef crop.

articles.text: Western Colorado is filling up with cattle, and what is noticeable about it is that there are none but the best blooded animals going in. In one year from now the western slope will have more of the Shorthorns, the Herefords, the Galloways and the Polled-Angus cattle than will all the plains country east of the mountains.—[Colorado Live Stock Record.
articles.summary: Clipping: blooded cattle in western Colorado.

articles.text: The Maine governor has been officially notified by the commissioners of contagious diseases that the foot and mouth disease which appeared in one or two places in that state last winter, has been entirely stamped ont. The quarantine was relieved May 16th, just three months from the date of the appearance of the disease. It is believed that there is not now in the United States a single case of genuine "foot and mouth disease."—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipping: foot and mouth disease stamped out in Maine.

articles.text: It is claimed by some who have had experience, that the hay made from wild prairie grass will not give horses the the heaves, says the National Stockmen. A gentleman who has lived in the West for many years says that he never saw horses affected with this disease until after the introduction of tame grass for meadows. Heaves may not be easily cured, but if farmers will wet the hay a very little and shake it well, it will remove the dust and in most cases prevent heaves. This is more important during dry windy weather of spring.—[Kansas L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipping: prairie hay and heaves in horses.

articles.text: Not one farmer in five who raises colts from mares that he works appears to realize that with the poor treatment given the colts they only do about half as well as they ought or would do if well kept. They are compelled to chase the mare back and forth over the farm or the roads to town for the half-rations of milk she is unable to exceed, owing to overwork and scant feed, and between the great fatigue and scanty nourishment they receive, the colts make a poor and scraggy growth going into winter quarters dilapidated and hidebound, a proper prey for vermin within and without later on.—[Kansas L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipping: neglect of colts.

articles.text: Now that the spring season for beef is upon our ranchmen, and grass cattle are moving to market, too much stress cannot be laid upon the class of beef to be sent. The grand demoralizer, the jayhawker, that runs down prices, is the half-fatted, long-legged, distended paunched steer, who has had filling enough from sappy grass to swell his stomach, but whose ribs are bare of fat. He is the boss rascal that fools his owner, hurts his shipment and lowers the price, starting from the ranch looking well, he reaches the shipping-pens the worse for wear and market—a scallawag. Cut such back, and leave him a month or two; send none if not well fatted; half ripe cattle ruin the markets, demoralize trade, and hurt the business. Prices already are none too good; thin stuff will bring them lower; but good, fat steers will always sell. Then wait until ripe before you gather your beef plums.—[Texas L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping: advice against shipping half-fat steers.

articles.text: The Cherokee Strip Live Stock Association and the Barber County Stock Growers' Association have had bills printed containing a warning to southern cattle drovers to keep on the trail and quarantine grounds, and not infringe on the rights of local stockmen. To be forewarned is to be forearmed, and the drover who knowingly and intentionally intrudes on the rights of the man who is holding wintered or domestic stock should, and undoubtedly will, be made to suffer the full penalty of the law, if nothing worse.—[Medicine Lodge (Kan.) Cresset.
articles.summary: Clipping: Kansas stock associations warn trail drovers.

articles.text: A foreigner who went West a year ago with more money than experience, but who is returning a wiser, albeit a poorer man, recently related to a Chicago reporter the story of his ventures in the cattle business. "Why," he said, in talking of a wicked partner he had met in Denver, "he began to bulldoze me from the very time we went into partnership. We started out on the range to count our cattle—we two—and took only a darkey cook with us. The first night we camped he proposed that we decide who should be the boss, and I said all right. He then called a meeting, consisting of himself, the darkey cook and me, to order and nominated me for chairman. I was elected and sat on a saddle. Then he moved that we proceed to the election of a boss for the firm and that the election be by ballot. The motion was carried, and he handed around his hat, putting in a ballot for himself. I started to vote and he stopped me, saying that the chairman couldn't vote unless there was a tie. Well I thought I'd get a chance to vote anyway when the cook but in his ballot, but when Routt handed him the hat the negro said he couldn't write and I was left without any show at all to get even, and he was elected boss. He is still bossing it."—[Las Animas Leader.
articles.summary: Clipping: humorous story of a greenhorn's cattle partnership.

articles.text: Comparing the business of breeding horses on the range with that of cattle raising, a correspondent of the Texas Live-Stock Journal says: "Horses are thriftier than cattle and require less range for their support. Some cattle men deny this, but the current of stockmen's testimony is to this effect, and it is sustained by the books, and by observation as well. The lips and teeth of the horse adapt it for cropping short herbage much better than those of the cow, and a horse can subsist where an ox would starve. Last winter, in riding over the country, I noticed quite a number of dead cattle but never a dead horse. Horses do not scatter and drift as much as cattle, and it is therefore much less trouble to gather and ranch them. In winter, when cattle are drifting south hundreds of miles, unless held in the face of the northers, a well located herd of horses will not ordinarily leave their accustomed range as much as five miles. Horses are not so branchy as cattle; not so troublesome to surrounding farms, or so obnoxious to farmers. Large numbers of cattle can not be satisfactorily kept in a vicinity interspersed with small farms. It would be folly in any one to think now of raising cattle on a large scale in this section unless held in pastures. Then, as ranges become scarcer, and numbers must be diminished, it is easier to keep the same amount of capital invested in the business by improving the breed of horses than cattle."—[National L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping: horse breeding compared with cattle raising.

articles.text: The Mark Lane Express, London, under date of April 28th, says: "In the 'Meat' columns of this journal last week, the opinions of some high authorities in the United States were cited in favor of the dead-meat trade. The New York Tribune declares that 'if dressed meat can be carried from Australia to England successfully, more than 12,000 miles, and across the tropics, it can be carried from Montana and Wyoming to the Eastern markets, or to England.' The Texas Live Stock Journal says: 'During the past year we have contended that true economy and best financial results, to accrue to our cattle interests, can be secured by building up the dead-meat trade to Great Britain.' The American National Live Stock Journal, and other papers, take the same view, while it is generally admitted that the dressed meat trade from the Western to the Eastern States has completely beaten the cattle traffic, in spite of the opposition of those interested in the latter. Mr. P. D. Armour, probably the largest meat man in the world, says: 'It stands to reason that when a steer has not been subjected to a ten days' feverish journey, and bruised and beaten in a cattle train, his flesh is the better for it. This meat ripens in transit. All this fuss against the fresh meat trade comes from these middle men. No consumer in this wide world has ever said aught against it.' Just so; and what is true about a ten days' journey by rail in America, is still more forcible in relation to a ten days' or a fortnight's passage over the Atlantic, in the stifling hold of a ship, and with the great rollers of the ocean tossing and mauling the wretched cattle for days at a stretch."—[National Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping: British and American opinion favoring the dressed-meat trade over live cattle shipment.

articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper arrived.

articles.summary: Coleman & Brown's restaurant nears completion.

articles.summary: S. Smith's freight outfit of two twelves arrived.

articles.text: One of Baldwin's mules got his foot caught in his lariat and was found dead.
articles.summary: One of Baldwin's mules was found dead, caught in its lariat.

articles.text: Jos. Ferris is building a large addition to his store and intends to add a line of groceries.
articles.summary: Jos. Ferris enlarges his store and will add groceries.

articles.text: Claude Ralph's outfit arrived Tuesday and loaded Wednesday, starting immediately for the Hills.
articles.summary: Claude Ralph's outfit loaded freight for the Black Hills.

articles.text: Get ready to trip the "light fantastic" in the theatre building, the evening of July 4th. Every one is cordially invited.
articles.summary: A dance is announced for the evening of July 4 in the theatre building.

articles.text: Mr. McNutt, a government contractor at Fort Custer was here last week for a few days and returned home Sunday night.
articles.summary: Government contractor McNutt of Fort Custer visited.

articles.text: A car load of nails arrived a few days ago for Star & Bullock. It awaits the arrival of their bull outfit from the Hills.
articles.summary: A carload of nails for Star & Bullock awaits their bull train from the Hills.

articles.text: The N. P. side-track is completed except for a little levelling. It is a great convenience in transacting the freight bnsiness.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific side-track at Medora is nearly finished.

articles.text: Baldwin's mule outfit has been loading about six thousand pounds of freight and will get its complement of 50,000 pounds soon.
articles.summary: Baldwin's mule train is loading freight.

articles.text: Mrs. T. G. Jones started Saturday morning for Spearfish, where she will reside for the future. She was accompanied by her father, Mr. Cable.
articles.summary: Mrs. T. G. Jones left to live in Spearfish.

articles.text: Jack Simmons is in town direct from Coeur D'Alene. He likes the prospects but says that of all the mines located, only half a dozen are being worked, all the rest being in litigation.
articles.summary: Jack Simmons reports on the Coeur d'Alene mines.

articles.text: The cattle for the Badger cattle Co. were branded and driven to the home ranch at the mouth of Beaver, Friday and Saturday. Mr. Woodford, one of the company came with the cattle to make final arrangements.
articles.summary: Badger Cattle Co. cattle branded and driven to the home ranch at the mouth of Beaver.

articles.text: Major W. A. Fonda has made up his mind to let his legal light shine over our citizens. Although we are a very peaceable community, there will be considerable legal work to be done and we prophecy a successful future for the genial Major.
articles.summary: Major W. A. Fonda will practice law in Medora.

articles.text: Vick Smith, one of the best of the hunters, trappers and scouts of the west, called on us Monday morning. Settlers are getting altogether too thick here for Vick, and he intends going to Alaska soon, stopping off awhile at Coeur D'Alene.
articles.summary: Hunter and scout Vick Smith called at the office and plans to go to Alaska.

articles.text: Dr. A. J. Morton, of Iowa and his father of South Heart, were in town last Friday. Dr. Morton was so pleased with our place that he intends to locate here. He is a graduate of the College of Physicians and Surgeons, at Chicago, and is undoubtedly an able practitioner.
articles.summary: Dr. A. J. Morton will locate in Medora as physician.

articles.text: Pat. Smith of Bismarck and John Belding of Deadwood, got off last night to take our stage line to the Hills, having been informed that it was running. As it was, the cayuse-buckboard line from Miles City received two more of the last few passengers it will have. They will return by our line.
articles.summary: Two travelers expecting a Medora stage to the Hills had to use the Miles City buckboard line.

articles.text: And now Max Bass, of Belfield, has been and gone and done it. The happy capturer of Max's heart is Miss Martha Geissel, of New York. Hereafter "Il Penseroso" will be debarred from the repertoire of the musical Max. May peace and prosperity attend the future of the newly-wedded couple.
articles.summary: Max Bass of Belfield married Miss Martha Geissel of New York.

articles.text: B. Welf, a well-known merchant of Deadwood, arrived Sunday morning. He has a large stock of millinery, fancy goods, dress goods etc., and intends to start into business as soon as he can make arrangements for the accommodation of his stock. He is just such an enterprising business man as is needed in a new town.
articles.summary: Deadwood merchant B. Welf arrived to open a dry-goods business.

articles.text: Owing to the confused looks of Dan Friedman, when he was caught trying to smuggle two side-saddles into town in a cattle car under the head of "Household goods and Furniture," we should judge he was going to commit bigamy, were it not for—but what in the world does he want of two side-saddles anyway?
articles.summary: Joke about Dan Friedman shipping two side-saddles as household goods.

articles.text: Now that the new billiard hall and theatre building is so near completion, a detailed description would be appropriate. It is located on lot 7, block 17, and creates a very favorable impression from the railroad, standing as it does in full view. The dimensions of the building are 24x75 and 26 feet high. There are two full stories, each being twelve feet clear. The siding is of rough board, paper and drop siding, giving it a handsome external appearance. The floor is double thickness of 3½ inch hard pine. There are three coats of plaster, the outside being a hard finish coat that makes the rooms extremely bright and cheerful. In the first story is the bar room and two club rooms lead off a hall extending to the rear. In the second story is the theatre, consisting of a large hall, a movable stage and two dressing rooms. There is a snug little balcony in front that adds materially to the fine appearance of the building. The total cost of the structure alone will probably over-run $4,500. The furniture will be in keeping with the building and Roberts & Co. are already receiving it. The opening will take place July 4, to which time all are looking forward for an enjoyable time.
articles.summary: Description of Medora's new billiard hall and theatre building, 24x75 feet on lot 7, block 17, to open July 4.

articles.text: The force-pump in the Marquis' garden is working in excellent shape and no more fear of drought troubles the brain of M. Eyraud.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès's garden force-pump is working, relieving M. Eyraud's drought worries.

articles.text: Twenty-five head and over of cattle are being slaughtered daily. A large number are coming in from the round-up and soon work will begin in earnest.
articles.summary: Twenty-five or more cattle slaughtered daily; more arriving from the round-up.

articles.text: Dr. Morton's card, published in our card column makes known the fact that we are to have a local physician, an advantage fully appreciated here from its lack hitherto.
articles.summary: Dr. Morton's card announces Medora's first local physician.

articles.text: As may be seen by their card, Messrs. McKenzie & O'Brien have formed a partnership in the blacksmithing business. It would be hard to find two better workmen and we are glad to state that they are rushed with work.
articles.summary: McKenzie & O'Brien form a blacksmithing partnership.

articles.text: Ira C. Bellows, of Mandan, was in Medora a few days last week. He has large interests in Mandan and is with good cause a firm believer in her future.
articles.summary: Ira C. Bellows of Mandan visited Medora.

articles.text: A party of Deadwood prospectors is on a trip north of here, looking for signs of gold. They are in search of the mine said to have been discovered by a man who was afterward killed by Indians while guiding a party of friends to the "find." Although the Bad Lands are liable to contain anything in the mineral kingdom, we are not banking very heavily on getting up a stampede from here.
articles.summary: Deadwood prospectors search north of Medora for a rumored lost gold mine.

articles.text: Messrs. Porter and Ralph, Mrs. John Flaherty and Miss Smith arrived Tuesday morning from Deadwood. Mrs. Flaherty and Miss Smith are going to the Coeur D'Alene to meet the former's husband, Mr. Porter is going to the States, while Mr. Ralph will return to Deadwood. The trip was made in six days and the team was never driven off a walk.
articles.summary: A party arrived overland from Deadwood in six days.

articles.text: Theodore Rosevelt, the young New York reformer, made us a very pleasant call Monday, in full cow-boy regalia. New York will certainly lose him for a time at least, as he is perfectly charmed with our free western life and is now figuring on a trip into the Big Horn country. He is perfectly non-committal on politics and the alleged interview with him, published in the St. Paul Pioneer Press, speaks more for the reporter's assininity than for his perspicacity.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt called at the Cow Boy office in cowboy dress, planned a Big Horn trip, and stayed non-committal on politics.

articles.text: Lloyd Robert's ranch, twelve miles up the river, was the scene last Sunday of as pleasant a gathering as we have attended for a long time. Lloyd's ranch is a revelation to one supposing that the only level ground in the Bad Lands is found on top of the buttes. There are about a thousand acres of sloping ground and about two thousand acres with a very gentle incline toward the river. Mr. Roberts' family entered into the spirit of the occasion and made every one feel perfectly at home. There was nothing to mar the enjoyment of the occasion although the symmetry of the editorial countenance was slightly deranged, owing to a misunderstanding with the cayuse as to which should stop first, he or the rider.
articles.summary: A gathering at Lloyd Roberts' ranch twelve miles up the river; the editor was thrown by his cayuse.
